title: Add the "action" and "method" attributes to <button>
body:
### What is the issue with the HTML Standard?

## Description

Currently, the `<button>` element supports the `formaction` and `formmethod` attributes, which let it change the `action` and `method`, respectively, of its parent `<form>`.  Buttons should also support the `action` and `method` attributes, which would allow the button to make HTTP requests without being wrapped in a form.

This is the second of the [Triptych Proposals](https://triptychproject.org/), three (relatively) modest additions to HTML that would make it much more expressive. The first of these three is [PUT, PATCH, and DELETE support](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/3577#issuecomment-2294931398). While button actions benefit greatly from the first proposal, it is not required to make this one worthwhile; even with limited method support, button actions can dramatically simplify web authorship.

Details, FAQs, and alternatives can be found in the [full proposal](https://triptychproject.org/proposals/button-actions), with some evidence of its utility excerpted below. A formal pull request will follow on shortly—we'd love to gauge implementer interest in the meantime.

## Examples

Supporting button actions makes common web patterns simpler, more secure, and more convenient for web authors, while also enabling more complex patterns that were previously impossible or prohibitively complex in HTML. 

### Authentication

One of the most common actions on the web, "logging out," cannot be properly modeled in HTML. With the addition of button actions, logout routes can be served from a single HTML element.

```html
<button action="/logout" method="POST">Logout</button>
```

The two most common workarounds for this missing functionality are to put the logout URL in a hyperlink, or to wrap the button in a form. The [logout link](https://triptychproject.org/proposals/button-actions#Use-Links%20Instead%20of%20Buttons) violates the GET method contract, which has been causing a [common prefetch mistake](https://xcancel.com/aidenybai/status/2023439731518792102) for decades now. The [form wrapper](https://triptychproject.org/proposals/button-actions#Wrap-The%20Button%20in%20a%20Form) is an obvious hack—no form data is being submitted—to compensate for the fact that buttons cannot independently make HTTP requests. It's needlessly verbose and pushes people to enhancing their buttons with JavaScript, which imposes no such restriction.

With the addition of PUT, PATCH, and DELETE methods to HTML, logouts can also use the DELETE method. Not only does this allow for idempotent retries, but it conveniently lets server authors put all authentication actions in at the same URL. In this way, logging in and out becomes POST-ing or DELETE-ing a session:

```html
<button action="/session" method="DELETE">Logout</button>
```

## Multi-action forms

Although the form wrapping hack can work for simple actions, it falls apart when you want to model multiple actions inside a form. Fortunately, button actions make this trivial. The following example shows a common interactive pattern on the web: editing a post.

```html
<form action="/posts/123" method="POST">
	<!-- Main form submission -->
	<textarea name="content">I read the news today; oh boy.</textarea>
	<button>Save</button>
	
	<!-- Additional actions -->
	<button action="/posts/123" method="GET">Cancel</button>
	<button formaction="/posts/123/draft" formmethod="POST">Save Draft</button>
	<button action="/posts/123/delete" method="POST">Delete Post</button>
</form>
```

The above form allows the user to take four different actions, all elegantly modeled with HTTP routes and methods, and no JavaScript:

* `POST /posts/123` - Update the post using the `textarea` content 
* `GET /posts/123` - Return to the original post, making no edits
* `POST /posts/123/draft` - Save the new post as a draft
* `POST /posts/123/delete` - Delete the posts 

Note that the `formaction` and `formmethods` are not made superfluous by the addition of button actions—instead, they complement each other. The form's action is altered when the request needs the value of the form, which it does to update the post or save it as a draft, but the button's direct action is used (and the form values discarded) when cancelling the change or deleting the post entirely. 

This example could be improved with PUT and DELETE methods, adding idempotency and removing the ["URL method" hack](https://triptychproject.org/proposals/form-http-methods#ad-hoc-uri-semantics) from the deletion action. Even without full method support, however, button actions dramatically improve the simplicity and composability of common webform patterns.
